title: Terms of Reference for Consultancy to Conduct Baseline Evaluation Eye Health Workforce Project
raw_text: TERMS OF REFERENCE CONSULTANCY TO CONDUCT BASELINE EVALUATION EYE HEALTH WORKFORCE PROJECT INTRODUCTION The Fred Hollows Foundation (The Foundation) is a secular non-profit public health organization based in Australia, which was founded in 1992 by eminent eye surgeon Professor Fred Hollows. The Foundation focuses on strengthening eye health systems and the treatment and prevention of avoidable blindness caused by cataract, trachoma, diabetic retinopathy, and refractive error. It operates in more than 20 countries across Australia, the Pacific, South and South-East Asia, and Africa. Since 2006, The Fred Hollows Foundation has worked in partnership with the Ministry of Health to advance Eye Health outcomes in Rwanda through systems strengthening, capacity building, and workforce development initiatives. These efforts have included sustained support for the training and professional development of ophthalmologists and allied eye health professionals. Building on the work FHF and MoH are doing on the integration side (Performance Based Financing) and Strengthening Systems for Eye Health (HSS), The Foundation, MoH and key stakeholders have jointly designed the Rwanda Eye Health Workforce Project (2026–2030) to strengthen the sustainability of Rwanda’s Eye Health System by addressing one of the most binding constraints to equitable, high-quality eye care in Rwanda: the shortage and maldistribution of well-trained ophthalmologists and the limited capacity of national training institutions to produce and retain them. 1. BACKGROUND AND CONTEXT The Rwanda Eye Health Workforce Project (RW26-01) is a five-year initiative (January 2026 – December 2030) funded by The Fred Hollows Foundation, implemented throughpartners including the Ministry of Health (MoH), the University of Rwanda (UR) and the Rwanda International Institute of Ophthalmology (RIIO) and other partners in eye health in Rwanda. The project responds directly to the severe shortage and inequitable distribution of ophthalmologists in Rwanda. The country has approximately one ophthalmologist per million population far below the WHO benchmark of one per 250,000 with most specialists concentrated in Kigali, leaving rural and underserved populations with limited access to essential eye care. Rwanda continues to face a significant burden of avoidable blindness and visual impairment, with cataract the leading cause of blindness and uncorrected refractive error the main cause of visual impairment. The National Strategy for Health Professions Development (NSHPD 2020–2030) sets an ambitious target of 44 public-sector ophthalmologists by 2030, and the Government’s 4- by-4 Health Workforce development Initiative aims to rapidly scale the health workforce. In alignment with these reforms, both RIIO (through its accredited residency) and UR (through its new Master of Medicine in Ophthalmology) are expanding national training capacity. The Workforce Project is designed to strengthen this pipeline, so that expanded training translates into competent, motivated, and equitably deployed specialists embedded within the public health system. The project purpose is to reduce avoidable blindness and visual impairment in Rwanda by strengthening the ophthalmology workforce pipeline (training, deployment, retention and leadership) to deliver equitable, high-quality eye care nationwide. The end-of-project outcome is a competent, equitably distributed, and sustainable ophthalmology workforce, fully embedded within the public health system and delivering high-quality, accessible eye care services across all provinces. The project is organized around three interlinked outcomes: Outcome 1: Increased supply of highly competent ophthalmologists graduating from nationally accredited training programs. Outcome 2: Improved deployment, retention, and motivation of ophthalmologists in public health facilities. Outcome 3: Strengthened leadership, partnerships, and research capacity addressing Rwanda’s eye health priorities. This baseline evaluation establishes the reference values, institutional capacity status, and system readiness against which the project’s progress will be measured at mid-term (2028) and end-term (2030). It is designed as an independent, primarily desk-based assessment that consolidates existing evidence, complemented by targeted key informant consultation, and is expected to be conducted between November to January 2027. 2. OBJECTIVES OF THE ASSIGNMENT The overall purpose of the baseline evaluation is to measure the status of the project prior to implementation, establishing a robust reference point against which performance will be monitored at mid-term and end-term. The evaluation will document the current capacity of institutions to train, deploy and retain ophthalmologists, and provide an evidence base to guide institutional strengthening and adaptive management. The specific objectives are to: Establish baseline values for the project’s outcome, output and activity indicators as set out in the Project Design Document (PDD), Monitoring, Evaluation, Research and Learning (MERL) framework, including those currently marked “TBD”. Validate and, where necessary, correct the baseline values already recorded in the PDD (see Section 4.3), so that a single baseline set is established. Propose SMART, evidence-based targets for all PDD indicators whose targets are currently marked “TBD”, benchmarked against national commitments. Assess the current institutional and training capacity of UR, RIIO and affiliated teaching hospitals against national, regional (COECSA) and international accreditation standards, including faculty numbers and skill mix, equipment and infrastructure, simulation/wet-lab capacity, educational resources, and quality assurance and student support systems. Assess the current status of workforce specifically ophthalmology deployment, distribution, retention and motivation across the public health system, including gaps affecting equitable placement beyond Kigali. Assess the baseline status of professional leadership, partnerships and locally led research capacity in the eye health sector. Review and align findings with existing national and sectoral evidence sources, and triangulate baseline values against these sources with clear references (see Section 3). 8. Identify key implementation gaps, risks, opportunities and priority actions the project should focus on to achieve its intended outcomes, ensuring alignment with national priorities and integration into Rwanda’s broader health workforce development system strengthening agenda. Provide practical recommendations to strengthen project design, targeting, sequencing, implementation, and the MERL framework. 3. SCOPE OF WORK / TASKS The evaluation covers the full scope of the Rwanda Eye Health Workforce Project (2026–2030) at national level, encompassing the two national training institutions (UR and RIIO), affiliated teaching and clinical training sites, and the public-sector deployment and retention environment for ophthalmologists across Rwanda’s 30 districts. The consultant will assess the baseline situation against each of the three project outcomes and will have autonomy to expand the indicative questions below to suit the evaluation. Alignment with existing evidence sources The consultant must review and align baseline findings with existing evidence sources, ensuring consistency, avoiding duplication of data collection, and clearly referencing the source of each baseline value. These sources include, but are not limited to: The Eye Care Service Assessment Tool (ECSAT) – for facility- and system-level service capacity, human resources and infrastructure data. Rwanda’s Eye Health Strategic Plan – the National Strategic Plan for Eye Health (NSPEH 2018–2024 and the successor plan 2025–2030 for national targets, priorities and coordination structures. Other available national and sectoral evidence, including the National Strategy for Health Professions Development (NSHPD 2020–2030) and the 4x4 Health Workforce Initiative; HSSP V (2024–2029) and the National Health Policy; RAAB (2015); the Gender Equity and Inclusion Analysis of Eye Care (2022); the Cataract Surgery Business Case (2023); UR and RIIO partner capacity assessments; COECSA minimum equipment and accreditation standards; the WHO IPEC framework and WHA 74.13; HMIS/DHIS2, PBF and CBHI/RSSB records; and ROS workforce records. Findings must be interpreted in a way that emphasizes alignment with national priorities and integration into Rwanda’s broader health system strengthening agenda, including the health workforce, service delivery, leadership and governance, and medical products and technologies pillars. Indicative evaluation of core and exploratory questions by outcome Outcome 1: Increased supply of highly competent ophthalmologists graduating from nationally accredited training programs. What is the current institutional and training capacity of UR, RIIO and affiliated teaching hospitals relative to COECSA and national accreditation standards (faculty numbers and skill mix, equipment and infrastructure, simulation/wet-lab capacity, educational resources, quality assurance and student support)? What is the current faculty-to-resident ratio, number of residents enrolled and graduating (disaggregated by gender and institution), and pass rate in regional/international certification examinations? What are the main gaps in training quality, standardization, surgical exposure (including MSICS) and subspecialty capacity that the project should prioritize? How effectively do the current training arrangements support the equitable recruitment, retention, and completion of residency training for women and residents with disabilities? What funding and financing mechanisms are available through the Government/MoH to support the training, deployment, and retention of ophthalmologists and other eye health. What is the current institutional and training capacity of relevant training institutions and affiliated clinical training sites to produce competent allied ophthalmic cadres (ophthalmic nurses, optometrists, ophthalmic clinical officers, refractionists), relative to national accreditation and professional standards including faculty availability, equipment and infrastructure, clinical training opportunities, educational resources, quality assurance systems and student support mechanisms? What is the current number of allied ophthalmic personnel enrolled in training programmes, graduating annually, and employed in the eye health sector (disaggregated by cadre, gender and institution), and what proportion successfully achieves professional certification, registration or competency assessment requirements? What are the main gaps in training quality, standardization, clinical exposure, practical skills development, continuing professional development, mentorship and specialized competencies among allied ophthalmic personnel that should be prioritized? How well do strengthened training arrangements support equitable access, progression, and successful completion of training for women and persons with disabilities across ophthalmology and allied eye health cadres? What is the status of the proposed OCO upgrading pathway and University of Rwanda Bachelor of Optometry programme, including their approval, implementation timelines, and confirmed positions of the MoH and other relevant regulatory bodies, in relation to NSPEH 2025–2029 workforce targets? Outcome 2: Improved deployment, retention, and motivation of ophthalmologists in public health facilities. What is the current number and distribution of ophthalmologists across provinces and rural/urban areas (disaggregated by gender and region), and how does this compare with population need, disease burden and NSHPD targets? What is the current retention rate of ophthalmologists in public service, and what factors (remuneration, working conditions, career pathways, incentives) drive attrition? To what extent are national deployment, bonding and compulsory-service policies in place and enforced, and how ready are receiving hospitals (eye team, equipment, consumables, maintenance and data systems) to support specialist practice? What deployment, retention and motivation mechanisms and/or strategies should the project prioritize to strengthen equitable distribution beyond Kigali for eye health professionals (e.g. ophthalmologists, allied cadres? What is the current number, cadre mix and geographic distribution of OCOs, ophthalmic/PEC nurses and optometrists (disaggregated by gender, province and facility level); how does this compare with NSPEH and NSHPD targets; and to what extent do reported changes in the OCO workforce reflect genuine attrition as opposed to register updates or reclassification, What are the deployment, retention and attrition patterns for allied cadres; what factors (remuneration, career progression, supervision, workload, working conditions, recognition) most influence them; and how well do current employment arrangements support equitable retention and career progression for women and persons with disabilities? What CPD and in-service training opportunities currently exist for OCOs and other allied cadres and how are they financed and quality assured; what has previously been delivered through The Foundation’s Accelerate and HSS/SSEH projects and by other partners; and where are the most significant unmet gaps that could be addressed through targeted, low cost interventions? What is the current number, cadre mix and geographic distribution of OCOs, ophthalmic/PEC nurses and optometrists (disaggregated by gender, province and facility level); how does this compare with NSPEH and NSHPD targets; and to what extent do reported changes in the OCO workforce reflect genuine attrition as opposed to register updates or reclassification, verified against regulatory council and MoH registers? What are the deployment, retention and attrition patterns for allied cadres; what factors (remuneration, career progression, supervision, workload, working conditions, recognition) most influence them; and how well do current employment arrangements support equitable retention and career progression for women and persons with disabilities? What CPD and in-service training opportunities currently exist for OCOs and other allied cadres and how are they financed and quality assured; what has previously been delivered through The Foundation’s Accelerate and HSS/SSEH projects and by other partners; and where are the most significant unmet gaps that could be addressed through targeted, low cost interventions? Outcome 3: Strengthened leadership, partnerships, and research capacity addressing Rwanda’s eye health priorities. What is the current status of professional leadership and networks (including ROS) and of active institutional and international partnerships supporting ophthalmology training and standards? What is the baseline level of locally led operational and clinical research capacity, output and evidence use for quality improvement? How effectively is eye health workforce development currently coordinated among MoH, UR, RIIO, ROS, ROCOCs, teaching hospitals and partners, and how well does it integrate into national planning, review and accountability mechanisms? How are allied and mid-level cadres registered, licensed and regulated; are career grade frameworks and progression pathways clearly defined; how effectively are these cadres represented by professional bodies (including ROCOCS); and to what extent are they reflected in national workforce planning, HRH information systems and performance-based financing arrangements? What are the most promising opportunities for The Foundation to support workforce development among allied cadres; which are sufficiently clear and MoH-aligned to be actionable in the near term and which require further clarity on national direction; which other partners are active or planning investment, and where are the risks of duplication or opportunities for complementarity; and what would be the indicative scale, cost, feasibility and likely service-delivery return? The consultant should consolidate findings from the exploratory questions into a standalone chapter or annex, concluding with a concise, prioritized summary of options for potential future engagement clearly distinguishing those actionable now from those contingent on further MoH clarity, and noting explicitly where the evidence base remains insufficient. Specific tasks Prepare an inception report and detailed methodology, including a baseline indicator matrix mapping each PDD indicator to its data source, and secure any required ethics review/approval. Conduct a structured desk review of the evidence sources listed above and extract baseline values, clearly referencing each source. Undertake targeted Focus Group Discussions and key informant interviews with MoH, UR, RIIO, ROS, teaching hospitals including ophthalmologists in training and practice, and relevant partners, and technical consultations to obtain any missing information required to finalize baseline values/number. Populate the baseline column of the PDD MERL framework, resolving “TBD” values where feasible and flagging any that require future primary data collection. Reconcile and validate the baseline values already recorded in the PDD, documenting any correction with justification. Analyse and triangulate findings, identify gaps and priority actions, and validate preliminary findings with FHF and stakeholders. Test the project assumptions and risks set out in the project design document 8. Produce draft and final baseline reports and disseminate findings to project stakeholders. Key Project Partners: Ministry of Health (Directorate responsible for Health Workforce; Department of Clinical Services) University of Rwanda (UR) – School of Medicine and Pharmacy / Department of Ophthalmology Rwanda International Institute of Ophthalmology (RIIO) Rwanda Ophthalmological Society (ROS) Rwanda Medical Council (RMC) and Rwanda Health Accreditation Agency (RHAS) • Rwanda Medical Association (RMA) and Human Resources for Health Secretariat (HRHS) Teaching and clinical training sites (CHUK, Kabgayi Eye Unit, Rwanda Charity Eye Hospital, Rwanda Military Hospital) Eye health partners including Cure Blindness Project (CBP), CBM, Fondazione Leonardo Del Vecchio, Orbis International and OneSight WHO Rwanda Country Office 4. METHODOLOGY AND APPROACH 4.1. Overall design Given the nature of this workforce project and the availability of substantial existing evidence, the baseline is designed principally as a desk-based assessment complemented by targeted qualitative consultation. The selected consultant will prepare a detailed methodology in collaboration with The Foundation teams (Rwanda and global teams) and will propose the most appropriate design; at a minimum, the methodology should be broad enough to accommodate both quantitative and qualitative methods. Information to answer the evaluation questions will be gathered through the following processes: Structured review of secondary data and existing evidence, including ECSAT outputs, the Rwanda Eye Health Strategic Plan (NSPEH), NSHPD 2020–2030, the 4-by-4 Initiative, RAAB (2015), the Gender Equity and Inclusion Analysis of Eye Care (2022), the Cataract Surgery Business Case (2023), UR and RIIO partner capacity assessments, and COECSA accreditation standards. Review of routine data systems, including HMIS/DHIS2, PBF, and training-institution and MoH/ROS, Rwanda Medical and Dental Council (RMDC) workforce records, the MoH-Health Workforce Management Systems (HWMS). Key informant interviews with MoH, UR, RIIO, ROS, RMDC, teaching hospitals and relevant eye health partners. Focus group discussions or technical consultations with faculty, residents and eye care teams, as appropriate, and sequenced after the key informant interviews so that emerging findings can be tested. 4.2 Equity and disaggregation The Fred Hollows Foundation will recruit an independent research consultant or institution to conduct the baseline evaluation. The consultant is expected to apply gender- and disability responsive approaches throughout, disaggregating data by sex, institution and region wherever feasible, and to triangulate across sources to ensure the reliability of baseline values. 5. KEY DELIVERABLES The following deliverables are expected from the consultant in completing the assignment: An inception/evaluation plan and methodology, including a baseline indicator matrix and timelines. Proposed quantitative and qualitative data collection tools (as part of the inception report) • Evaluation of ethics review and approval (where applicable). Completed data collection tools aligned to the evaluation questions and PDD indicators. A populated baseline indicator matrix (PDD MERL framework baseline column) with referenced sources. Presentation and validation of preliminary findings. Draft and final baseline evaluation reports, including an executive summary and a summarized slide deck for dissemination of findings. All raw data collected/generated during the evaluation, provided in an agreed and accessible format, with a backup provided to The Foundation. The Foundation will provide the following: A designated focal person to coordinate and support, the consultant. Documents required for the desk review in its possession include the project design documents and reports, MERL framework, and advocacy plan. Consolidate feedback on all draft deliverables including the evaluation plan, methodology, data collection tools, reports, and other deliverables. Support for introductions and coordination between the consultant and partners/stakeholders throughout the evaluation. Support for the logistics of the validation session(s). 6. DURATION AND TIMELINE The baseline evaluation is expected to commence in December 2026 for an estimated duration of 45 working days, covering desk review, key informant interviews, analysis, report writing, and final presentation to FHF. The indicative schedule is set out below. No Activity Person Responsible Indicative Date 1 Finalization of Baseline Evaluation TOR MERL Team 20th October 2026 2 Contracting / consultant recruitment Contracts & Procurement Team 15th November 2026 3 Ethics review (as applicable) Consultant 20th November 2026 4 Inception report and methodology Consultant 30th November 2026 5 Review of secondary information (desk review) Consultant 07th December 2026 6 Focus Group Interviews Consultant 15th December 2026 7 Key informant interviews / technical consultations Consultant 15th December 2026 8 Data analysis and synthesis Consultant 20th December 2026 9 Draft baseline report and validation of findings Consultant 10th January 2027 10 Internal dissemination of Baseline Evaluation Results Consultant 20th January 2027 11 Final baseline report and presentation to stakeholders Consultant 30th January 2027 7. REPORTING AND SUPERVISION The evaluation is commissioned by The Fred Hollows Foundation. The consultant will work under the day-to-day guidance of and report to the FHF MERL Manager, who will coordinate access to documents, partners and stakeholders and consolidate feedback on all deliverables, with technical oversight from the FHF Global Support Team (Development Effectiveness / MERL), and in close collaboration with the Senior Workforce Project Manager and Senior Program Manager. The primary intended users of the baseline report are The Foundation’s Programs Division (including the Program Development Team and country program teams), the Rwanda Team, the Country Support Network, and the Development Effectiveness Team. Secondary users include the Ministry of Health, the University of Rwanda, RIIO, ROS, and other eye health sector partners. All deliverables are subject to FHF review and approval, and the consultant is expected to incorporate feedback within agreed timelines before signing off. 8. REQUIRED QUALIFICATIONS AND EXPERIENCE This evaluation will be contracted to an independent evaluator or team who will work closely with The Foundation staff in the design and implementation of the evaluation. Where a team is proposed, it must collectively demonstrate the capabilities below, and the technical proposal must name each member with their specific role and level of effort. The Foundation seeks to engage an independent individual or registered organization with the following experience and expertise: At least a master’s degree in medicine, Public Health, Ophthalmology, Health Workforce Development/Human Resources for Health, or a related health-sciences discipline. Possession of a PhD in a relevant field will be an added advantage. Demonstrable experience in the evaluation of public health programmes, including health systems and health workforce assessments, particularly in Eye Health. Demonstrated understanding of higher education systems and health professional training institutions, including faculty development, residency and postgraduate training programmes, accreditation standards, curriculum implementation, and academic governance. Experience working within a university, teaching hospital, academic department, or professional training institution will be considered a strong advantage. Proven experience in developing and using quantitative and qualitative data collection tools and evaluation methods, including desk-based and mixed-methods approaches. • Strong knowledge of and experience working with the Rwandan health care system, health workforce reforms (including the 4x4 reform Initiative and NSHPD) and health sector policies. Familiarity with eye health, ophthalmology training/accreditation standards (e.g., COECSA) and workforce planning are an added advantage. Strong analytical skills and demonstrated ability to synthesize evidence from multiple sources. Excellent spoken and written communication skills in English, and demonstrated Kinyarwanda fluency within the team 9. APPLICATION PROCESS AND EVALUATION OF PROPOSALS 9.1: Submission requirements Interested individuals or institutions should submit a cover letter, curriculum vitae/company profile, and technical and financial proposals to The Foundation office in Rwanda. Submissions should reference “Consultancy to Conduct the Baseline Evaluation for the Rwanda Eye Health Workforce Project (RW26-01)” and send to the following address: rwanda@hollows.org. Only submissions with complete documents as stated in the TOR and those meeting minimum requirements will be considered. Qualified consultants will be subjected to a background check for compliance including on child protection, as a condition for engagement. Qualified consultants may be subject to a background check on child protection as a condition of engagement. The Foundation reserves the right to accept or reject any application and is not bound to provide reasons for its decision. 9.2: Evaluation criteria Proposals will be assessed on a combined technical and financial score, weighted by 70:30. Only proposals scoring 70 or above on the technical criteria will have their financial proposal opened. Evaluation Criterion Weight (%) Component Understanding of the assignment, the Rwandan eye health sector, and the health workforce development context 15 Technical Soundness and feasibility of the proposed methodology, including data collection, analysis approach, validation process, and approach to resolving TBD indicators and setting targets 25 Technical Team composition, relevant qualifications, academic and technical expertise, understanding of health professional education and faculty development, health workforce capability, report writing and language proficiency (English and Kinyarwanda) 20 Technical Demonstrated experience conducting comparable evaluations of health workforce, health systems strengthening, medical education, specialist training, or public health programmes 20 Technical Realism and quality of the proposed workplan, staffing plan, and level of effort against the stated timeline 10 Technical Equity, gender, disability inclusion, and stakeholder engagement approach 10 Technical Technical Subtotal 100 Weighted 70% Itemized financial proposal demonstrating value for money and cost realism 100 Weighted 30% Final Combined Score 100 70% Technical + 30% Financial Note: The successful consultant(s) will be required to satisfactorily complete compliance, safeguarding, and due diligence screening prior to contract award. The Foundation reserves the right to accept or reject any proposal without obligation to provide justification. Experience working with academic institutions, teaching hospitals, postgraduate medical and public health education, faculty and curriculum development, accreditation systems, specialist health workforce training programmes, or health professional education systems will be considered an asset during the evaluation process. 10. MANAGEMENT AND LOGISTICS This evaluation is being commissioned by The Fred Hollows Foundation Rwanda. The Rwanda program team will work closely with the selected consultant(s), providing coordination support, access to documentation and facilitation of stakeholder engagement throughout the assignment. The technical proposal should demonstrate understanding of the assignment, a proposed methodology and workplan, and relevant experience. The financial proposal should present a detailed, itemized budget. 11. CONFIDENTIALITY The consultant(s) agree not to divulge confidential information to any person for any reason during or after completion of this contract with The Foundation. Upon completion or termination of this contract, the consultant(s) undertake to return to The Foundation any materials, files or property in their possession that relate to the work of The Foundation. The consultant will be responsible for the safety, security and administration of primary and secondary data collected from FHF or otherwise. 12. INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY All intellectual property and/or copyright material produced by the evaluator(s) whilst under contract to The Foundation remains the property of The Foundation and will not be shared with third parties without the express permission of The Foundation. The evaluator(s) are required to surrender any copyright material created during the term of the contract to The Foundation upon completion or termination of the contract. 13. SAFEGUARDING PEOPLE The Fred Hollows Foundation is committed to ensuring that its activities are implemented in a safe and productive environment which prevents harm and avoids negative impacts on the health and safety of all people, particularly children, vulnerable people, and disadvantaged groups. The Foundation has a zero-tolerance approach to sexual exploitation, abuse, and harassment of any kind. All personnel, including contractors/consultants, are expected to uphold and promote high standards of professional conduct in line with The Foundation’s Safeguarding People Policy including Code of Conduct. Contractors/consultants will be expected to sign and adhere to The Foundation’s Safeguarding Code of Conduct and provide any background checks as required. 14. INSURANCE Any consultants involved in this evaluation will be required to have in place insurance arrangements appropriate to provision of the requirements in this Terms of Reference, including travel insurance. 15. ETHICAL AND OTHER CONSIDERATIONS The evaluator and evaluation team are expected to maintain high professional and ethical standards and comply with The Foundation’s Research and Evaluation Policy. The Foundation is committed to ensuring a safe environment and culture for all people, including children, with whom we come in contact during our work. All members of the evaluation team will be required to comply with The Foundation’s Safeguarding People Policy and sign the Safeguarding Code of Conduct.

title: Terms of Reference (ToR) for the Consultancy to Develop Adolescent Health Audio-Visual Materials for the National ASRH Programme
raw_text: CALL FOR PROPOSALS PLAN/ FY27/10/001 Terms of Reference (ToR) for the Consultancy to Develop Adolescent Health Audio-Visual Materials for the National ASRH Programme 1. Background The National Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health (ASRH) Programme aims to improve adolescents’ knowledge, access to quality services, and adoption of positive health behaviors. To support national training, awareness creation, and behavior change communication, there is a need for high-quality, youth-friendly, culturally appropriate, and inclusive Adolescent Health (AH) audio-visual materials. These materials will be aligned with national policies and guidelines and used by the Rwanda Biomedical Center (RBC), implementing partners, and other stakeholders. 2. Purpose of the Consultancy The purpose of this consultancy is to develop technically accurate, engaging, and validated adolescent health audio-visual materials to support national ASRH training, communication, and community engagement activities. 3. Scope of Work Under the overall coordination of the Rwanda Biomedical Center and with procurement and financial management by Plan International Rwanda, the consultant will undertake the following tasks: A. Script Development Develop clear, youth-friendly, and gender-responsive scripts covering priority adolescent health and Sexual Reproductive Health Rights (SRHR) topics. Ensure alignment with national Adolescent Sexual Reproductive Health (ASRH) policies, standards, and cultural context. B. Script Review and Validation Workshop Organize and facilitate a script review workshop with approximately 15 ASRH/SRHR experts, including youth representatives, for 3 days. Revise and finalise scripts based on consolidated feedback. C. title: Request for Proposals (RFP) for the Recruitment of a Consultancy to Conduct a Digital Market and Digital Skills Gap Assessment Across the Sama Countries
raw_text: TERMS OF REFERENCE Request for Proposals (RFP) for the Recruitment of a Consultancy to Conduct a Digital Market and Digital Skills Gap Assessment across the SAMA Countries (Under the Smart Africa Markets for All (SAMA) Programme, Across the six SAMA countries: Benin, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Zambia) Client / Contracting entity Smart Africa Secretariat 10th Floor, Career Centre Building KG 541 ST, Kigali, Rwanda, P.O. Box: 4913 Tel: +250 788 300 581/+250788822155 Email: tenderenquiries@smartafrica.org | www.smartafrica.org RFP # 157/S.A/SAMA/RFP/10/2026 Programme Smart Africa Markets for All (SAMA) Assignment title Digital Market Gap and Opportunity Analysis and Digital Skills Gap Assessment for the Digital Market, SAMA Interventions 1 and 2 Assignment structure One consultancy awarded as a single package comprising two coordinated components. Bidders must demonstrate distinct technical expertise for each Component and may propose a consortium or specialist team arrangements to ensure adequate depth across both components. A single contract will be awarded for the full assignment. Geographic coverage Benin, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Zambia Languages English and French, with local-language data collection where required Release date 08/10/2026 Closing date 09/11/2026 at 17:00 Kigali time (CAT / UTC+2) Contact Enquiries: tenderenquiries@smartafrica.org |Submissions: procurement@smartafrica.org Introduction and General Background 1.1 About the Smart Africa Alliance The Smart Africa Alliance is a bold and innovative commitment from African Heads of State and Government to accelerate sustainable socio-economic development on the continent, with the vision of transforming Africa into a Single Digital Market by 2030. Established through its Manifesto, a collaborative effort among African nations, the African Union, the Economic Commission for Africa, the African Development Bank, the World Bank, the International Telecommunication Union, the private sector, and academic and research institutions, the Alliance was endorsed by African leaders in 2014 and has since garnered the support of 42 African countries representing over one billion people. The Smart Africa Secretariat, headquartered in Kigali, Rwanda, coordinates continental programmes that support digital market integration, policy harmonization, institutional strengthening, and innovation-ecosystem development across Member States, placing information and communications technologies at the core of national and continental socio-economic development. More information: https://smartafrica.org 1.2 About Smart Africa Markets for All (SAMA) Programme Smart Africa Alliance curated the Smart Africa Markets for All (SAMA), an initiative that brings in nexus between digital innovation – entrepreneurship, digital skills and knowledge, and strengthening policy and regulatory environment for digitization of markets while impacting youth with a particular focus on young women. SAMA Programme is a four-year, multi-country initiative supported by the Mastercard Foundation, running from 2026 through 2029. The Program aims to unlock dignified and fulfilling work opportunities for 35,584 young people, with a target of 70% young women, 5% persons with disabilities, and 5% refugees/internally displaced persons, by improving access to digital markets for economically disadvantaged youth, particularly young women small traders. The Programme is implemented across six countries: Benin, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Zambia. The program responds to systemic challenges in Africa’s informal economy, where approximately 90% of workers are informal and youth, who make up 75% of the population, face interlinked barriers such as limited digital connectivity, financial exclusion, inadequate market access, and digital skills gaps. SAMA builds on Smart Africa’s existing digital initiatives such as SANIA, SADA, SATA, SWG etc and aligns with the organisation’s vision for Africa’s Single Digital Market by 2030 as well as the African Union’s vision, ensuring that program efforts complement broader continental strategies for inclusive digital transformation. 1.2.1 SAMA Strategic Pillars SAMA is built around three interconnected strategic pillars to drive inclusive growth: a) Entrepreneurship and digital innovation, b) Youth Digital Skills, and c) Institutional Capacity Building. In practice, this translates to: Accelerating Inclusive Digital Innovation by supporting youth-led tech solutions that reduce market barriers for informal traders. Youth Digital Skills Development by providing digital, financial and entrepreneurial skills training to young persons, especially young women, to improve their employability and enterprise growth. Strengthening Institutions and Policy by working with governments and regional bodies to harmonize policies, improve regulatory environments, and build institutional capacity for a unified digital market. 1.2.2 SAMA Target Personas The Programme’s human-centred design is built around and targets three distinct groups of young persons in Africa: Small market trader or “Aisha”: As a young woman and small market trader who struggles to make ends meet selling from a tabletop in her local market. She represents the millions of economically disadvantaged youths in informal trade who need access to markets, financial inclusion, and digital tools to improve their livelihood. To benefit from the digitalization happening around her, Aisha needs training to effectively and safely use digital tools, and she needs digital products and services tailored to her realities as a young woman small trader, so that she can move from the periphery to the center of the digital economy. Social techpreneurs or “Chebet”: A recent university graduate or young social digital entrepreneur who develops inclusive digital solutions responsive to Aisha’s realities. She embodies the entrepreneurial spirit of university educated youth eager to leverage digital innovation for social impact but needs support to succeed. While she may not be as economically disadvantaged as Aisha, she has limited financial, technical, and business support to pursue social entrepreneurship. Chebet’s success is directly connected to Aisha because her enterprise is intended, first and foremost, to develop inclusive digital solutions tailored to the needs and realities of small traders such as Aisha. Unemployed disadvantaged youth or “Nala”: Nala is a young person from a low-income household who faces difficulty accessing meaningful employment and seeks ICT training to improve her work prospects. She represents the youth seeking to acquire digital skills to improve their employability and access opportunities in the growing digital economy. While she may not be as economically disadvantaged as Aisha, she is from a low-income community and not able to find a job easily. With access to relevant training, certification and employment pathways, she could find better work as tech worker or even upskill her current tech skills to obtain industry-related certification and employment pathways in the emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, cloud computing, data science and coding etc. 1.2.3 SAMA Programme Interventions Intervention 1: Accelerating Inclusive Digital Innovation: This intervention focuses on supporting young social techpreneurs like Chebet pursue entrepreneurship to develop homegrown digital solutions that respond to the market barriers experienced by small traders like Aisha to stay in business and thrive in digital markets. Chebet groups will receive relevant digital, tech and entrepreneurship skilling and training. The Programme will support 200 young social techpreneurs to pursue entrepreneurship and develop approximately 80 digital solutions that enable small traders to remain in business, access markets and participate more effectively in the digital economy. This will be carried out in Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Ghana. Intervention 2 – Skilling Young Talents for employability and future of work. This intervention focuses on developing the digital skills of 48,000 young people in Benin and Zambia to prepare them for the future of work either as digital entrepreneurs or tech talent. It comprises two distinct skilling pathways: foundational digital-literacy, financial-literacy and entrepreneurship training for 30,000 small traders like Aisha delivered in-person. While advanced digital skills modules such as cybersecurity, AI, Cloud, data science etc) will be delivered in a hybrid format to 18,000 disadvantaged young people like Nala. Intervention 3 – Strengthening institutions and policy This intervention focuses on enabling policy and regulatory environment to drive inclusive digital transformation across Africa in which the digital innovation and skills interventions can translate into improved economic participation and work opportunities, particularly for young women small traders like Aisha. This intervention works with governments, regulators, and regional bodies to strengthen institutional capacity, develop inclusive policies and regulations, address barriers within digital markets, and advance policy harmonization and interoperability. Consultancy Purpose and Objectives 2.1 Purpose of this Assignment Digital markets, including mobile money, digital payments, e-commerce, social commerce, logistics platforms and other technology-enabled services—can enable informal micro and small traders to reach wider markets, improve transaction efficiency, strengthen customer relationships and increase the resilience and growth of their enterprises. However, participation in and sustained use of these services remain uneven, particularly among economically disadvantaged young women operating within informal and small-scale trade. Young women small traders like Aisha face interconnected barriers that drive them to the margins of digital economy. These may include limited access to affordable digital devices and connectivity, low digital and financial literacy, inadequate access to finance, limited trust in digital platforms, exposure to fraud and online harm, unsuitable platform design, logistics constraints, restrictive social norms, care responsibilities and limited access to appropriate learning and business-support services. These barriers affect not only whether traders adopt digital tools, but also whether they can use them safely, productively, and consistently to improve their livelihoods. Under Intervention 1: Accelerating Inclusive Digital Innovation, SAMA’s implementing partner, GrowthAfrica Foundation, will support 200 young social techpreneurs like Chebet through ideation, incubation and acceleration to develop approximately 80 homegrown digital solutions that respond to the market barriers experienced by informal micro and small traders like Aisha. Without robust evidence on the small traders’ lived experiences, existing behaviours, unmet needs and market conditions, there is a risk that innovation activities may be based on assumptions or produce solutions that are not sufficiently relevant, accessible, affordable or responsive to the target users’ realities. SAMA therefore requires country-specific evidence on how informal micro and small traders currently participate in digital markets; the products and services they use, attempt to use or abandon; the barriers affecting adoption and sustained use; and the market opportunities that inclusive digital solutions could address. The findings will be translated into prioritised challenge areas, problem statements, design criteria, personas and user journeys for use by GrowthAfrica and the Chebet cohorts during ideation, hackathons, incubation and acceleration. Under Intervention 2: Skilling Young Talents for Employability and the Future of Work, SAMA seeks to strengthen the digital, financial and entrepreneurial capabilities required by young people to participate in the digital economy. For this assignment, the Digital Skills Gap Assessment shall examine foundational competencies for Aisha-aligned small traders and advanced digital skills and employment-readiness needs for Nala-aligned disadvantaged youth. For Nala, it shall also assess realistic pathways from training into work, particularly in Benin and Zambia. The assessment is required to establish the digital, financial and entrepreneurial competencies currently possessed by different seller segments; identify the skills gaps that constrain digital-market participation; assess the relevance, accessibility and quality of existing skilling provision; and recommend appropriate competency levels, learning pathways, curriculum priorities, delivery modalities, partnerships and inclusion and safeguarding measures. The findings will directly inform the design and contextualisation of seller-focused skilling interventions implemented by NetOne Foundation in Zambia and Pigier Foundation in Benin. For Nala-aligned youth, the findings will also inform how the advanced digital-skills training offered by NetOne Foundation and Pigier Foundation can connect to verified job opportunities and appropriate employer or placement partners. The two evidence needs are closely interconnected. Digital solutions may fail to achieve adoption where traders lack the necessary skills, confidence, devices, trust, or ongoing support. Similarly, digital-skilling interventions may have limited effect where available products, platforms and services are unaffordable, inaccessible, unsafe, or poorly adapted to traders’ realities. Assessing these dimensions through one coordinated consultancy will enable SAMA to develop a coherent evidence base connecting trader needs, digital-market barriers, solution-development opportunities and digital-skilling priorities. Because the evidence needs of Interventions 1 and 2 are closely connected, this assignment will be implemented as a one multi-country consultancy comprising of two distinct, but interrelated components delivered under a single contract: Component 1: Digital Market Gap and Opportunity Analysis among small traders Component 2: Digital Skills Gap Assessment of small traders Both components shall use common definitions and a shared analytical framework to allow comparison across countries and between the two interventions. In addition to generating evidence for programme design, the assignment shall establish baseline reference values for SAMA indicators and outcome domains that can be validly measured through the Digital Market Gap and Opportunity Analysis and the Digital Skills Gap Assessment. These will include digital-market participation and adoption, digital readiness, digital, financial and entrepreneurial competencies, access and inclusion barriers, and other relevant pre-intervention conditions. The findings will inform refinement of the SAMA MEL framework and subsequent participant-level baseline measurement. The strategic value of this assignment is to create a common evidence base linking market barriers, user needs, digital-solution opportunities and skills requirements, so that Interventions 1 and 2 reinforce each other rather than operate as separate workstreams. 2.2. Objectives of the assignment The overall objective is to generate a comprehensive, actionable and comparable evidence across the six SAMA countries, on digital-market adoption, barriers, unmet needs and opportunities among small traders (like Aisha) and on the digital, financial and entrepreneurial skills required by formal and informal sellers for effective participation in digital markets; and to translate the findings into design-ready inputs for inclusive digital solutions, competency-based skilling interventions and establish relevant baseline reference values to strengthen the SAMA programme MEL framework; and identify viable post-training employment pathways for Nala-aligned youth, including the skills, credentials and support needed to access them. 2.2.1 Specific Objective The specific objectives of the assignment are to: Map the current state of digital market adoption among informal micro and small traders in each SAMA country, including the digital platforms, products and services currently used, attempted or abandoned. Identify, segment and prioritize barriers, unmet needs and market opportunities affecting micro and small traders’ adoption and sustained use of digital markets, including structural, financial, social, technical, gender-related, accessibility, safety, policy and regulatory barriers factors, and assess the relevance and suitability of existing digital solutions. Translate the digital-market findings into design-ready inputs for inclusive innovation, including validated thematic challenge areas, sector-by-theme matrices, prioritized problem statements, design considerations, personas and user journeys to inform Intervention 1’s hackathon tracks, challenge briefs and incubation support for “Chebet” cohorts. Assess the foundational digital, financial and entrepreneurial competencies of Aisha-aligned small traders, and the advanced digital-skills and employment-readiness needs of Nala-aligned disadvantaged youth, taking into account differences across countries and beneficiary segments (disaggregated by sex, age, disability status, displacement status, seller type and location.) Assess the existing digital-skilling ecosystem for both pathways, including training providers, curricula, certification options, employer demand and partnership opportunities, and identify gaps and overlaps affecting learner progression. Develop a practical competency framework prioritized and country-contextualized recommendations translating the identified gaps into competency levels, learning pathways, priority training modules, delivery modalities, targeting, sequencing, partnerships, inclusion measures and monitoring indicators. Identify and assess viable post-training job pathways for Nala-aligned youth in Benin and Zambia, informed by employer and industry demand, entry-level roles, hiring requirements, recruitment channels, work quality and the barriers facing young women and other underserved youth; recommend practical links between SAMA training, certification and access to work. Establish baseline reference values for relevant SAMA indicators and outcome domains measurable through the two assessments, with appropriate definitions and disaggregation, and provide recommendations for their integration into the SAMA MEL Framework. Scope of the Assignment The assignment shall be implemented as one coordinated, multi-country consultancy comprising two distinct but interrelated components. Component 1: Digital Market Gap and Opportunity Analysis among small traders Component 2: Digital Skills Gap Assessment of small traders Both components shall cover Benin, Zambia, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda and Uganda; and shall generate country-specific findings, cross-country comparisons and consolidated recommendations. In addition to the diagnostic requirements under each Component, the consultant shall establish baseline reference values for relevant SAMA indicators and outcome domains that can be validly measured through the two assessments. Baseline measures shall be embedded within the respective Work Packages rather than undertaken as a separate study. Indicators requiring longitudinal tracking of actual SAMA participants or supported enterprises shall be baselined separately at enrolment, prior to substantive programme support. The consultant shall support this process by developing or refining the relevant participant and enterprise intake tools as part of the MEL alignment component. The scope of work shall be delivered through a common inception process, the Work Packages under each Component, and cross-cutting requirements applicable to the assignment, as set out below: 3.1 Inception and Integrated research design The consultancy firm shall undertake a common inception process covering both components to confirm the analytical approach, research design, baseline measurement requirements and implementation arrangements before assessment begins. The consultants shall: Review relevant SAMA programme documents (including the SAMA Impact Measurement Priorities), national and regional policies, existing studies, administrative data and other available relevant evidence; Refine the analytical framework, research questions, operational definitions and methodology for each Component; Map the SAMA indicators and outcomes domains relevant to components 1 and 2 against the research questions and identify the baseline reference values that can be generated through the assessment under each Component Develop country-specific sampling plans, respondent sample frames and stakeholder-engagement strategies for both components; Develop core and Component-specific data collection instruments (toolkits); Develop the fieldwork, data quality-assurance, ethics, safeguarding, inclusion and data-management protocols; and Submit a validated Inception Report and detailed workplan for approval by Smart Africa and partners. 3.2 Component 1: Digital Market Gap and Opportunity Analysis (Intervention 1) Component1 shall assess how informal micro and small traders engage with digital markets, identify the barriers, unmet needs and opportunities affecting their adoption and sustained participation, and translate the findings into design-ready inputs for inclusive digital solutions under SAMA Intervention 1. The assessment shall also generate relevant baseline reference values on digital-market participation, adoption, inclusion and related enterprise-market conditions that support SAMA’s impact pathway and MEL framework. Component 1 shall be delivered through the following Work packages. Work Package 1: Mapping Digital Market Adoption and existing digital solutions Purpose: Establish how informal micro and small traders currently participate in digital markets and use existing digital products, platforms and services across the six SAMA countries. Key Tasks: Review existing evidence on micro/small trade, and digital-market participation in each Country. Map the digital platforms, products, and services currently used, attempted, or abandoned by small traders like Aisha (including digital payments, e-commerce, social commerce, logistics platforms, and relevant digital business tools). Assess patterns and levels of use, including the purpose, frequency, intensity, and stage of adoption. Assess small traders’ experience with these digital solutions, including usability, relevance, inclusion, affordability, accessibility, safety, reliability and interoperability and other design factors. Compare digital market participation and adoption patterns across countries, sectors, locations, business maturity and relevant trader segments. Deliverable: Digital Market Adoption Analysis Report Work Package 2: Barriers, Unmet Needs and Opportunity Analysis Purpose: identify, segment and prioritise the barriers, unmet needs affecting small traders’ adoption and sustained participation in the digital markets; and identify opportunities for inclusive digital solutions and relevant policy action. Tasks: Identify and analyse structural, financial, technical, social, gender-related, accessibility, safety, policy and regulatory barriers) affecting digital market participation by the small traders. Assess the barriers across the adoption journey, including awareness, access, affordability, trust, initial use and sustained use of digital products and services. Examine how the identified barriers and unmet needs vary by country, market type, sector, location, business maturity and relevant demographic characteristics of small traders. Prioritise the identified barriers and unmet needs based on their prevalence, severity and implications for the small traders’ digital market participation and enterprise growth. Identify and assess market opportunities and recommend areas where new or improved digital products, services or business models could better respond to small traders' needs. Produce a country-specific and cross-country sector-by-theme barrier matrix linking priority barriers and unmet needs to market opportunities and regulatory considerations. Deliverable: Barriers, Unmet Needs and Opportunity Prioritisation Report Work Package 3: Design-Ready Synthesis for Inclusive Innovation Purpose: Translate the evidence generated under Work Packages 1 and 2 into practical, design-ready inputs that Chebet Cohorts in Intervention 1 can use to develop inclusive digital solutions responsive to small traders' needs. Tasks: Synthesize the findings into thematic challenge areas and priority opportunity areas for inclusive digital innovation Develop clear, evidence-based problem statements, describing priority challenges experienced by small traders. Develop design considerations and user requirements to guide the development of accessible, affordable, safe and relevant digital solutions. Develop or refine Aisha personas (small market trader) and user journeys reflecting different trader segments, contexts, barriers, and digital market experiences. Package the findings into practical inputs for hackathon tracks, challenge briefs and incubation support for Chebet cohorts. Deliverable: Design-Ready Innovation Package 3.3 Component 2: Digital Skills Gap Assessment for the Digital Market (Intervention 2) Component 2 shall assess the digital, financial and entrepreneurial competencies required by formal and informal small traders to participate effectively, safely and productively in digital markets; identify existing competency gaps and skilling needs; and translate the findings into practical inputs for the design and contextualization of SAMA’s small-trader (Aisha focused) skilling interventions. The assessment shall also generate relevant baseline reference values on digital competencies, digital readiness, and inclusion that support the SAMA impact pathway and MEL framework. In line with the two skilling pathways under Intervention 2, Component 2 shall address both the foundational digital, financial and entrepreneurial competencies of Aisha-aligned small traders and the advanced digital-skills needs of the Nala target group (including modules such as cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, cloud computing and data science), so that the competency framework and recommendations inform both skilling pathways. For the Nala pathway, the assessment shall connect advanced digital-skills priorities with available routes into work after training, particularly in Benin and Zambia. This Component 2 shall be delivered through the following Work Packages: Work Package 4: Digital Skills and Competency Gap Assessment Purpose: establish current digital, financial and entrepreneurial competencies, of small traders aligned with Aisha target group and determine the competencies required for effective, safe, and productive participation in digital markets in the six SAMA Countries. Key Tasks: Identify and validate relevant small market trader (Aisha) segments based on characteristics such as seller type, business maturity, digital readiness, sector, location and other factors influencing skilling needs. Assess the current digital, financial, and entrepreneurial competencies for formal and informal small traders aligned with Aisha target group, including competencies relevant for effective participation in the digital markets and enterprise growth. Identify the gaps between the small traders’ current competencies and those required for effective, safe, and productive participation in the digital market across six SAMA Countries. Assess how identified competency gaps affect key business practices including use of digital tools for marketing, payments, customer engagement, record-keeping and enterprise management, etc. Determine the competencies required at different levels of digital-market participation. Present skills gaps across countries and seller segments disaggregated appropriately (country, seller type, sector, business maturity, location and relevant demographic characteristics, including age, disability and displacement status. Prioritise competency areas requiring strengthening for different Aisha segments. Assess the advanced digital-skills needs of Nala-aligned youth, including priority skill areas, current competency levels, barriers to progression, certification pathways and employment-readiness requirements for entry-level digital roles. Deliverable: Digital Skills and Competency gap assessment report Work Package 5: Digital Skilling Ecosystem Assessment Purpose: map the existing digital skilling ecosystem relevant to small market trader (Aisha), identify gaps in current provision, overlaps and partnership opportunities. Tasks: Map existing digital skilling providers, programmes and curricula relevant to small market traders aligned with the Aisha in the six SAMA countries. Review the competency areas and training content currently offered and assess their alignment with the priority competency needs identified under Work Package 4. Identify gaps in existing skilling provisions, including gaps in competency coverage, content, accessibility, delivery approaches, reach, learner support etc. Identify opportunities in the existing skilling ecosystem and recommend areas for adaptation, partnership or strengthening to inform the design and delivery of SAMA’s Aisha-focused skilling intervention. For the Nala pathway, assess employer and industry demand for advanced digital skills in Benin and Zambia, including priority entry-level occupations, role-specific competencies, relevant certifications, experience requirements and recruitment practices. Map and validate realistic post-training job pathways for Nala-aligned youth, including entry-level paid employment, internships and apprenticeships, and, where supported by evidence, remote or freelance digital work. Consult employers, industry bodies, recruitment or placement intermediaries and training providers to identify current and emerging opportunities, entry conditions, remuneration and work-quality considerations, barriers to access and potential hiring or referral partnerships. Distinguish verified opportunities from anticipated demand; the assignment does not include placing participants in jobs or guaranteeing vacancies. Deliverable: Digital Skilling Ecosystem and Nala Job Pathways Report Work Package 6: Competency Framework and Recommendations Purpose: translate the findings into a usable competency framework and actionable recommendations for Aisha-focused skilling and Nala-aligned youth progression from advanced digital-skills training into work. Tasks: Develop two connected competency pathways: one for foundational digital-market participation by Aisha-aligned traders, and one linking advanced digital-skills training, certification and employment readiness to validated post-training job pathways for Nala-aligned youth. Translate the identified competency gaps into appropriate learning pathways and priority modules. Recommend training content, sequencing, and delivery modalities suited to the needs and context of different Aisha Segments. Recommend appropriate targeting, learners’ support, accessibility, inclusion, and safeguarding measures to support Aisha’s participation and progression. Recommend relevant partnership options and monitoring indicators for the Aisha-focused skilling intervention and, for Nala, employer engagement, placement or referral mechanisms and measures of transition into dignified and fulfilling work. Deliverable: Digital Competency Framework with Skilling and Nala Job Pathways Recommendations 3.4 Baseline Reference Values and MEL Alignment Baseline measurement shall be embedded within the relevant Work Packages under components 1 and 2. The consultant shall design the research tools to capture, calculate and record the applicable baseline reference values identified in Annex 1: Proposed Baseline Indicator Matrix, aligned with the relevant SAMA Impact Measures and the SAMA MEL framework. Applicable measures shall be consistently defined and appropriately disaggregated in accordance with the requirements set out in Annex 1. The resulting reference values, calculation methods, and underlying datasets shall be documented for integration into the SAMA MEL system. The consultant shall establish baseline values for the relevant programme indicators in Annex 1. The baseline methodology shall explain, for each indicator: indicator operational definitions; baseline measurement methodology; calculation formula; baseline assumptions; sampling for each indicator; disaggregation; and Indicator verification. Ensure baseline-relevant measures are structured so they can be repeated in subsequent MEL measurement using comparable definitions and response categories. 3.5 Cross-Cutting Requirements Apply gender-responsive and inclusion-sensitive research approaches, aligned with the SAMA monitoring and evaluation framework. Disaggregate findings consistently by sex, age, disability status, displacement status, seller type, sector and location, where sample size and respondent safety permit. Observe ethical research standards, including informed consent, safeguarding, confidentiality, data protection, and secure data management. Ensure instruments and field protocols are accessible and culturally appropriate, including reasonable accommodation for persons with disabilities. Use harmonized core instruments and definitions across countries and across both components, while allowing justified country-specific modules. Clearly distinguish between evidence, interpretation and recommendations, and document study limitations. Avoid duplication with Intervention 3: policy and regulatory issues should be assessed only where they directly affect digital-market participation, solution adoption or skilling outcomes under Interventions 1 and 2. Comply with Smart Africa's data-protection, consent and safeguarding requirements: sign a data-protection agreement with Smart Africa before any fieldwork begins; use Smart Africa's informed-consent form; and observe Smart Africa's safeguarding rules for any contact with young people. The relevant templates will be shared by Smart Africa. 3.6 Main Deliverables Inception Report and approved tools Fieldwork/Data Collection Package Draft Component 1 Report + Design-Ready Innovation Package Draft Component 2 Report + Competency Framework, Skilling and Nala Job Pathways Recommendations Baseline Reference Values/MEL Package Validation and consolidated synthesis Final Assignment Package Methodology and Sampling The consultant shall propose an appropriate mixed-methods methodology for undertaking both components across the six SAMA countries. The detailed methodology, sampling approach and data-collection tools shall be refined and agreed with Smart Africa during the inception phase. At the minimum, the methodology shall include Type of Data Methodology Target Group / Source Primary data Quantitative survey/assessment A statistically justified sample of formal and informal small traders aligned with the Aisha target group across the six countries. The sample shall allow relevant country-level analysis and disaggregation. Focus Group Discussions / participatory methods Small traders from different Aisha segments, including young women and men and, where relevant, persons with disabilities and displaced populations. Key Informant Interviews Relevant digital-market actors, digital and financial service providers, skilling providers, employers, industry bodies, recruiters or placement intermediaries, government/regulatory stakeholders and other relevant ecosystem actors. Secondary data Desk review SAMA programme and MEL documents, national policies and strategies, existing studies, administrative data, market and digital-economy evidence, and relevant skilling-sector information. The consultant shall ensure that: data-collection tools address the specific research questions under Components 1 and 2, capture the agreed baseline reference measures and examine the availability, entry requirements and accessibility of post-training job pathways for Nala-aligned youth; the proposed sample adequately reflects relevant differences by country, location, sector, seller type, business maturity and Aisha segment; relevant findings are disaggregated by sex, age, disability and displacement status, where applicable; quantitative, qualitative and secondary evidence is triangulated; and All methods comply with the assignment requirements on ethics, safeguarding, accessibility, informed consent, data protection and data quality. The consultant shall provide the proposed sampling design and indicative sample size for each data-collection method in the technical proposal, with the final sample approved during inception. Deliverables and Indicative Timeline The consultant shall deliver the following. Deliverables are submitted as integrated packages covering both components, with clearly separated Component-specific content where required. raw_text: TERMS OF REFERENCE Request for Proposals (RFP) for the Consultancy Services to Assess and Address the Policy, Regulatory and Interoperability Barriers that Prevent Young People from Participating in Digital Markets (KYC, Digital e-Services, Interoperability and Data Exchange across Six African CountriesUnder the Smart Africa Markets for All (SAMA) Programme) Client Smart Africa Secretariat 10th Floor, Career Centre Building KG 541 ST, Kigali, Rwanda, P.O. About Smart Africa The Smart Africa Alliance is a bold and innovative commitment from African Heads of State and Government to accelerate sustainable socio-economic development on the continent, with the vision of transforming Africa into a Single Digital Market by 2030. Established through its Manifesto, a collaborative effort among African nations, the African Union, the Economic Commission for Africa, the African Development Bank, the World Bank, the International Telecommunication Union, the private sector, and academic and research institutions, the Alliance was endorsed by African leaders in 2014 and has since garnered the support of 42 African countries representing over one billion people. The Smart Africa Secretariat, headquartered in Kigali, Rwanda, coordinates continental programmes that support digital market integration, policy harmonization, institutional strengthening, and innovation-ecosystem development across Member States, placing information and communications technologies at the core of national and continental socio-economic development. More information: https://smartafrica.org 2. The Smart Africa Markets for All (SAMA) Programme Smart Africa Alliance curated the Smart Africa Markets for All (SAMA), an initiative that brings in nexus between digital innovation – entrepreneurship, digital skills and knowledge, and strengthening policy and regulatory environment for digitization of markets while impacting youth with a particular focus on young women. SAMA Programme is a four-year, multi-country initiative supported by the Mastercard Foundation, running from 2026 through 2029. The Program aims to unlock dignified and fulfilling work opportunities for 35,584 young people, with a target of 70% young women, 5% persons with disabilities, and 5% refugees/internally displaced persons, by improving access to digital markets for economically disadvantaged youth, particularly young women small traders. The Programme is implemented across six countries: Benin, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Zambia. The program responds to systemic challenges in Africa’s informal economy, where approximately 90% of workers are informal and youth, who make up 75% of the population, face interlinked barriers such as limited digital connectivity, financial exclusion, inadequate market access, and digital skills gaps. SAMA builds on Smart Africa’s existing digital initiatives such as SANIA, SADA, SATA, SWG etc and aligns with the organisation’s vision for Africa’s Single Digital Market by 2030 as well as the African Union’s vision, ensuring that program efforts complement broader continental strategies for inclusive digital transformation. 2.1 SAMA Strategic Pillars SAMA is built around three interconnected strategic pillars to drive inclusive growth: a) Entrepreneurship and digital innovation, b) Youth Digital Skills, and c) Institutional Capacity Building. In practice, this translates to: Accelerating Inclusive Digital Innovation bysupporting youth-led tech solutions that reduce market barriers for informal traders. Youth Digital Skills Development byproviding digital, financial and entrepreneurial skills training to young persons, especially young women, to improve their employability and enterprise growth. Strengthening Institutions and Policy by workingwith governments and regional bodies to harmonize policies, improve regulatory environments, and build institutional capacity for a unified digital market. 2.2 SAMA Target Personas The Programme’s human-centred design is built around and targets three distinct groups of young persons in Africa: Small market trader or “Aisha”: Asa young woman and small market trader who struggles to make ends meet selling from a tabletop in her local market. She represents the millions of economically disadvantaged youths in informal trade who need access to markets, financial inclusion, and digital tools to improve their livelihood. To benefit from the digitalization happening around her, Aisha needs training to effectively and safely use digital tools, and she needs digital products and services tailored to her realities as a young woman small trader, so that she can move from the periphery to the center of the digital economy. Social techpreneurs or “Chebet”: A recent university graduate or young social digital entrepreneur who develops inclusive digital solutions responsive to Aisha’s realities. She embodies the entrepreneurial spirit of university educated youth eager to leverage digital innovation for social impact but needs support to succeed. While she may not be as economically disadvantaged as Aisha, she has limited financial, technical, and business support to pursue social entrepreneurship. Chebet’s success is directly connected to Aisha because her enterprise is intended, first and foremost, to develop inclusive digital solutions tailored to the needs and realities of small traders such as Aisha. Unemployed disadvantaged youth or “Nala”: Nala is a young person from a low-income household who faces difficulty accessing meaningful employment and seeks ICT training to improve her work prospects. She represents the youth seeking to acquire digital skills to improve their employability and access opportunities in the growing digital economy. While she may not be as economically disadvantaged as Aisha, she is from a low-income community and not able to find a job easily. With access to relevant training, certification and employment pathways, she could find better work as tech worker or even upskill her current tech skills to obtain industry-related certification and employment pathways in the emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, cloud computing, data science and coding etc. 2.3 SAMA Programme Interventions Intervention 1: Accelerating Inclusive Digital Innovation: This intervention focuses on supporting young social techpreneurs like Chebet pursue entrepreneurship to develop homegrown digital solutions that respond to the market barriers experienced by small traders like Aisha to stay in business and thrive in digital markets. Chebet groups will receive relevant digital, tech and entrepreneurship skilling and training. The Programme will support 200 young social techpreneurs to pursue entrepreneurship and develop approximately 80 digital solutions that enable small traders to remain in business, access markets and participate more effectively in the digital economy. This will be carried out in Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Ghana. Intervention 2 – Skilling Young Talents for employability and future of work. This intervention focuses on developing the digital skills of 48,000 young people in Benin and Zambia to prepare them for the future of work either as digital entrepreneurs or tech talent. It comprises two distinct skilling pathways: foundational digital-literacy, financial-literacy and entrepreneurship training for 30,000 small traders like Aisha delivered in-person. While advanced digital skills modules such as cybersecurity, AI, Cloud, data science etc) will be delivered in a hybrid format to 18,000 disadvantaged young people like Nala. Intervention 3 – Strengthening institutions and policy This intervention focuses on enabling policy and regulatory environment to drive inclusive digital transformation across Africa in which the digital innovation and skills interventions can translate into improved economic participation and work opportunities, particularly for young women small traders like Aisha. This intervention works with governments, regulators, and regional bodies to strengthen institutional capacity, develop inclusive policies and regulations, address barriers within digital markets, and advance policy harmonization and interoperability. 3. About this Assignment 3.1 What we are asking for We want to know, country by country, exactly what stops a young entrepreneur, particularly a young woman from entering a digital market, operating in it, and growing beyond her own locality or national border.
